title: my creative barrier reef ecosystem
content:
on creative process | from my sketchbook

 

I used to believe that my creative practice was something that lived deep within me, at the very heart center — like an inner refuge or sanctuary that I could retreat to, when the outside world felt like too much. recently, I realized that this model was insufficient — because it implied a divide between inner (creative) and outer environments, when all creative work is ultimately about being in active conversation with life. sometimes this conversation is playful; sometimes, it is painful.

my creative practice is not a secret place I disappear into; it is the active process by which I create my experience of the world. it is weaving together the many threads and layers of my psychic membrane.

my creative practice is not a monastery I hide in, away from the world; it is how I make being in the world — in this human experience — bearable, even beautiful. it is the way by which I breathe, metabolize, touch, and be touched by the world. it is like having lungs outside of my body, or my own astronaut oxygen helmet. I inhale, I exhale. it is not a nice to have. I need it to breathe.

creative practice as ecosystem + barrier

the idea of a barrier reef came to me as I was thinking about living ecosystems that serve as both protective barriers, and as rich, dense ecosystems in themselves.

a barrier reef is formed very slowly, over time, as tiny corals form from around volanic islands. those volanic islands subside while the coral polyps grow towards the sunlight, forming lagoons between the ocean and the shoreline. it has two distinct purposes:

  1. a barrier reef absorbs the incoming force of waves before it reaches the shoreline.

  2. it creates rich habitats for marine ecosystems — both in the reefs, and in the protected waters of the lagoon.

in this metaphor, if my creative process/practice is the barrier reefs, then what is the ocean? what is land? what am I protected from? who am I protecting?

  
 

it might feel obvious to say that I’m protecting my core sense of self (land) from the uncertain onslaught of life/world (ocean waves) — through my creative practice (barrier reefs).

I could also say that I’m protecting my sensitive psyche (ocean waves) from the fleshy, earthly material world (land) through creative practice (barrier reefs). however, both of these explanations feel a bit too binary and simplistic to me.

unconscious + conscious realms

for me, the ocean feels symbolic of the realm of the unconscious / psychic / creative / imaginal — to which I dare to voyage into, anytime I allow myself the pleasure of sinking into a creative practice.

land is the conscious, material and cognitive experience. it is the physical counterpart and manifestation of energy, submerged feelings, storylines, and intentions.

therefore, I can say that I am both — I am the ocean and I am the land. I am the relentless chaotic waves of emotion and experience, and I am my material being, decisions, my actions. my creative practice is the slowly forming coral reefs — through which I slow down my internal experiences; process, metabolize, and understand them.


barrier as transitional space

my creative practice forms a barrier ecosystem between my imaginal and material realms. they make the transition between the conscious/unconscious feel more gentle — by absorbing the enormous creative force of the oceanic realms. afterall, psychic energy can be absolutely terrifying. we need a buffer zone; a liminal place. barriers — or boundaries — are not about keeping separate, or creating division; it is about absorption and digestion. it is not a steel wall. instead of keeping things out — barriers are places of absorption — so that we can invite life in. it is about active digestion.

my creative barrier reefs serve as the liminal zone, where creative process is the means by through I bring what I sense and excavate from the unconscious depths — into the light of the conscious, then, into material reality. this metabolism process forms creative organisms (my creations), and eventually, they interact to form a rich, biodiverse ecosystem that flow back into the waters that I breathe in, everyday.

 
 

creating environments for growth

coral reefs are extremely slow growing — therefore, they’re highly vulnerable to disruptive forces of climate change and human activities. they also need specific conditions to grow: water temperatures, water clarity (for sunlight to reach it, and photosynthesis from algae), the right water chemistry, and movement (for nutrients/oxygen/detox).

for most of my life — I’ve been so obsessed with creating the right environmental conditions for my creative process. but the right environment isn’t any one particular thing — it’s not a perfect system, routine, schedule, or 5-step plan. there is no recipe. trying to force one thing would make creative life fragile and brittle, while the right conditions are some combination of chemistry

  • temperature — a container, an environmental feeling of safety

  • clarity — nourishment from sunlight, spaciousness

  • chemistry — inspiration, a spark, a fire, an urge

  • movement — breathing room, motion, openness to life/world


the focus is not on forcing output / creations / reefs to grow — they will organically grow at their own slow pace — but instead, on creating the most nourishing environment possible. usually, for me, this involves some combination of the right containers (time, form, medium, practice) and sensitivity to energy (momentum, flow, resistance).

returning to the practice

over the years, I see that I have created a thriving creative barrier reef ecosystem — and I feel it viscerally in my body and psyche when I haven’t tended to that practice in a while — especially if my system is processing a lot in my life.

so many things feel like they threaten a creative practice: life admin, interpersonal obligations, health issues, money anxieties, travel overwhelm, bad moods, sudden bouts of depression, angst of the world, the exhaustion of emotional labor, aka, all the sediments of being human.

but, I’ve learned from experience that when creating feels hardest, it’s when I need it the most — even just a tiny droplet. long periods of not tending to my practice feels like a slow suffocation — my mind becomes a soggy sponge, then a carnivorous flower, then a blue screen of death. if I try to be a “normal” person, normality just makes me feel more crazy. I don’t even understand how normal people exist in this world.

creative resilience

what comforts me to remember is that — despite their slow growth, sensitivity, and vulnerability, barrier reef ecosystems are resilient. most of this is from genetic/ecological diversity and adaptive mechanisms that have evolved over time.

which, metaphorically translated — I take to mean that we build creative resilience not through forcing one way, one practice, one form, one identity, one way of making XYZ — but to allow the mysteries of creative process be in its own organic unfolding.

it is always experimentation; it is a forever-dance what we cannot fully know, understand, or control. (I mean, how can you presume to know the mysteries of the ocean, and everything that lives in the deep??)

this is what we do in Labyrinth, and this is literally what I obsess about, everyday. when I feel the presence of my creative barrier ecosystem, I feel held by my own abundance. even — or especially — when all else in my life feels painfully hard, my creative barrier ecosystem makes me feel held by life.
